tally.headline: 3 of 12 gradeable claims held up, 8 did not

implied_side.why: EdgeDesk’s own number sat 1.1 points toward Jacksonville Jaguars of the quote EdgeDesk captured at Caesars. That is what the disagreement implied. It was published as research, not as a recommendation to bet it.

implied_total.why: EdgeDesk’s fair total of 43.9 sat 1.6 points below the captured total of 45.5.

closing_line.note: The line did not move between the captured quote and the close.

reasons: 8 of 10 gradeable claims went the other way. The read of this matchup was wrong in its mechanism, not only in its number.
EdgeDesk projected a home margin of 4.1 and the game finished 29 the home way — 24.9 points of margin error, OUTSIDE the range the model published.
process.basis: the drivers, matchups and measured advantages only — never the price or the market claim, which are the result in longer words

variance_markers.label: A two-turnover edge
variance_markers.text: Jacksonville Jaguars won the turnover battle by two, which is worth roughly a touchdown of scoreboard on average and is largely noise game to game.

variance_markers.label: A 29-point margin
variance_markers.text: Once a game is this far apart both teams stop playing the game they were rated on — the leader runs clock, the trailer throws — so late-game rates describe the situation rather than either team.

verdict.line: THE NUMBER LANDED AND THE REASONING DID NOT. This is the most dangerous result on this page, because it pays and teaches nothing. Nothing below should be read as EdgeDesk having understood this game.

grading.separation_note: The bet result and the process grade above are computed separately and are allowed to disagree. A winning number with a broken thesis is recorded as exactly that.

lessons.pregame_expectation: 1 of the claims in this article rested on model.
lessons.actual_result: None of them could be graded: no single-game statistic in EdgeDesk’s vocabulary observes this driver.
lessons.lesson: EdgeDesk prices these games partly on signals it has no way to observe afterwards. That is not an error in the model — it is a gap in the audit, and it means the platform cannot tell, from results alone, whether those parts of the number are earning their weight.
lessons.suggested_investigation: Consider whether a postgame data source exists for model.

lessons.actual_result: It graded a win. The reasoning behind it did not hold: 8 of 10 gradeable claims went the other way. The read of this matchup was wrong in its mechanism, not only in its number.
lessons.lesson: A winning number built on a reading the game contradicted. Nothing about this result should increase confidence in the mechanism EdgeDesk named, and treating it as confirmation is how a model gets worse while its record gets better.
lessons.suggested_investigation: Why did the number land while the mechanism failed? Either the number was right for a reason EdgeDesk has not identified, or it was luck. Both are worth knowing and they are different.

lessons.pregame_expectation: The model published an outcome range of -13.0 → +21.0 (Jacksonville Jaguars).
lessons.actual_result: The game finished outside it, at a margin of 29.
lessons.lesson: The published range is meant to contain eight results in ten. A miss is expected roughly twice in ten games and is only a problem in aggregate — which is exactly what this store exists to measure.
lessons.suggested_investigation: Count range misses across the season. A rate materially above 20% means the model’s stated uncertainty is too narrow.
